settings.heading: When the packet doesn't fit the person.
settings.body: Manufactured medicines come in fixed strengths and fixed forms. Compounding is what happens when your prescriber needs something else — a smaller dose, a liquid instead of a tablet, a cream instead of a capsule, or a formula without the ingredient you react to. A pharmacist makes it, one batch, for you.

settings.title: Something else
settings.body: Tell us and we'll route it

settings.heading: Five kinds of problem we solve most often.

settings.question: Do I need a prescription?
settings.answer: For anything Schedule 4 or 8, yes. S3 lines need a short conversation with a pharmacist. Over-the-counter lines you can order directly.

settings.question: How long does compounding take?
settings.answer: Most oral liquids and creams are ready within 24 to 48 hours of pharmacist approval. Sterile preparations take longer, and we tell you when we approve the script.

settings.question: Can you flavour a child's medicine?
settings.answer: Yes — strawberry, banana or unflavoured, in a sugar-free, dye-free base. We label the syringe in millilitres so there is no tablet-splitting maths at bedtime.

settings.question: Is a compounded medicine TGA registered?
settings.answer: No. Compounded medicines are made for one patient and sit outside the registration pathway. That is why a pharmacist reviews every script personally.
